top_locations.title: Great Zimbabwe
top_locations.snippet: Great Zimbabwe is the largest stone ruin in sub-Saharan Africa south of the Sahara, and one of the most important archaeological sites on the continent. Built between the eleventh and fifteenth centuries, it was the capital of a wealthy Shona trading state that controlled gold...

top_locations.title: Gonarezhou
top_locations.snippet: Gonarezhou — the name means "place of many elephants" in Shona — is Zimbabwe's second largest national park and arguably its wildest. Sprawling across 5,000 square kilometres of the southeastern lowveld, it sits at the junction of Zimbabwe, Mozambique, and South Africa, formin...

top_locations.title: Harare
top_locations.snippet: Harare is Zimbabwe’s capital and largest city, set at about 1,500 metres on the central plateau. It has been through very difficult times — hyperinflation, political repression, economic collapse — and the city shows the scars. But it remains a surprisingly green and pleasant...

top_locations.title: Bulawayo
top_locations.snippet: Bulawayo is Zimbabwe's second largest city, with a population of around 700,000, and the economic and cultural capital of Matabeleland. It's a slower, more relaxed city than Harare — the wide tree-lined streets were laid out on a generous colonial grid, and the pace of life in...

top_locations.title: Mutare
top_locations.snippet: Mutare is the largest town in Zimbabwe's Eastern Highlands, situated in a narrow valley near the Mozambique border with forested mountains rising on all sides. It is the commercial centre for the region and a practical base for exploring some of Zimbabwe's most spectacular hig...

top_locations.title: Lusaka
top_locations.snippet: Lusaka is the capital city of Zambia. It doesn't have the headline sights of some African capitals, but it's a sprawling, energetic place that rewards a few days of exploration -- and it's a practical base for sorting out documents and planning onward travel across the region.

top_locations.title: Ndola
top_locations.snippet: Ndola is the capital of Zambia's Copperbelt, tucked into the crook of the country against the Congolese border. It is the second-largest city in Zambia and the main stop between Lusaka and Kitwe. The economy runs on copper — the mines have been here since the colonial era, and...

top_locations.title: Kitwe
top_locations.snippet: Kitwe is the commercial heart of Zambia's Copperbelt, the second-largest city in the country and the hub of an industry that has shaped the nation's economy for nearly a century. It sits at around 1,300 meters elevation, giving it a surprisingly pleasant climate for a city thi...

top_locations.title: Shibam
top_locations.snippet: Shibam is known as the "Manhattan of the Desert" — and when you first see it rising from the floor of the Hadramawt valley, the nickname makes sense. top_locations.title: Baraqish
top_locations.snippet: Baraqish is an ancient city close to Marib and can be visited as a day trip from there. Located in the semi-arid area on the road to Hazm Al-Jawf, about 125 km from Sana'a, Baraqish stands on top of a lofty hill enclosed by a highly fortified wall up to 8 metres high in places...

top_locations.title: Hadramawt
top_locations.snippet: Hadramawt is a vast wadi region in eastern Yemen, stretching about 560 kilometres from the Arabian Sea to the Saudi border. It is one of the most spectacular landscapes in the Arabian Peninsula — a deep canyon cut through a limestone plateau, with ancient mud-brick tower citie...

top_locations.title: Sanaa
top_locations.snippet: Sana'a is one of the most extraordinary cities in the Arab world — a place where the architecture has barely changed in a thousand years and where even the new quarters have the feel of somewhere very old. The city sits in a high valley at about 2,200 metres, ringed by rugged...

top_locations.title: Aden
top_locations.snippet: Aden is Yemen's main port and former southern capital, built in and around the crater of an extinct volcano on a peninsula jutting into the Gulf of Aden. It has a long history as a trading hub — the British made it a strategic coaling station and free port in the 19th century,...

top_locations.title: Socotra
top_locations.snippet: Socotra is one of the most alien landscapes on Earth. This remote archipelago in the Indian Ocean, closer to the Horn of Africa than to the Yemeni mainland it technically belongs to, has been isolated long enough to evolve a flora found nowhere else — most famously the dragon...

top_locations.title: Hoi An
top_locations.snippet: Hoi An is a remarkably well-preserved ancient trading port on the central Vietnamese coast, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. For several centuries it was one of Southeast Asia's most important commercial hubs, drawing merchants from China, Japan, and the West — a history stil...

top_locations.title: Phong Nha - Ke Bang
top_locations.snippet: Phong Nha - Ke Bang is a 200,000-hectare national park in central Vietnam's Quang Binh province, straddling the eastern flank of the Truong Son range near the Laotian border. It was recognised as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2003, and again in 2015, for a reason that only f...

top_locations.title: Hue
top_locations.snippet: Hue was the imperial capital of Vietnam for nearly 150 years under the Nguyen Dynasty, and the city still carries that weight. The Perfume River bisects the city — the massive Citadel and Imperial Enclosure sit on the north bank, while the French colonial quarter, markets, and...

top_locations.title: Ho Chi Minh City
top_locations.snippet: Ho Chi Minh City — still called Saigon by almost everyone who lives there — is the commercial heart of Vietnam. It is louder, hotter, and more chaotic than the capital Hanoi a thousand kilometres to the north, and that is most of its appeal. Ten million people, an ocean of mot...

top_locations.title: Mekong delta
top_locations.snippet: The Mekong Delta is the southern rice bowl of Vietnam. The Mekong River — known to the Vietnamese as Song Cuu Long, the River of the Nine Dragons — originates high on the Tibetan plateau and flows through China, between Myanmar and Laos, along the Lao-Thai border, and through...

top_locations.title: Ha Long Bay
top_locations.snippet: Ha Long Bay is one of the most spectacular natural landscapes in Asia. Over 1,900 limestone islands and karst formations rise from the Gulf of Tonkin in the northeastern corner of Vietnam, draped in green jungle and riddled with caves, creating a seascape that looks like a Chi...

top_locations.title: Ninh Binh
top_locations.snippet: Ninh Binh is where Vietnam goes vertical. The province sits 90 km south of Hanoi and is carpeted with limestone karst towers — the same dramatic geology as Ha Long Bay, except here the peaks rise from rice paddies and slow rivers instead of ocean. The effect is extraordinary:...

top_locations.title: Halong City
top_locations.snippet: Halong City (formerly Hon Gai) is the provincial capital of Quang Ninh Province and the main gateway to Halong Bay — the UNESCO World Heritage-listed seascape of karst limestone islands that is one of Vietnam's most famous landscapes. The city sits on the bay's northern shore...

top_locations.title: Cat Ba Island
top_locations.snippet: Cat Ba is the largest island in Halong Bay, and it gives you something the bay's famous overnight cruises rarely offer: a place to actually stay and explore on your own terms. Most travelers pass through on a tour, but those who linger discover limestone karsts from the water,...

top_locations.title: Haiphong
top_locations.snippet: Haiphong is Vietnam's third-largest city and its most important port, sitting on the Cam River delta about 100 km east of Hanoi. top_locations.title: Hanoi
top_locations.snippet: Hanoi is one of Southeast Asia's most captivating capitals — a city where ancient temples sit next to French colonial villas, motorbikes swarm through streets barely wide enough for a bicycle, and the smell of pho drifts from every corner. As Vietnam's capital and second-large...

top_locations.title: Sapa
top_locations.snippet: Sapa is a hill station in the far north-west of Vietnam, set at 1,600 metres in a spectacular valley surrounded by the Hoang Lien Son mountains — the highest range in Indochina, culminating in Fansipan (3,143 m), Vietnam's tallest peak. The French built it as a mountain retrea...

top_locations.title: Ba Be National Park
top_locations.snippet: Ba Be National Park, in Bac Kan province about 250 km north of Hanoi, is centred on Ba Be Lake — the name means "three lakes", though the lake is a single continuous body of water 8 km long and up to 800 m wide. At 178 m above sea level, it is Vietnam's only significant natura...

top_locations.title: Hoa Binh
top_locations.snippet: Hoa Binh sits 75 km southwest of Hanoi at the edge of Vietnam's northwestern highlands, where the Red River Delta gives way to limestone mountains and terraced valleys. The provincial capital is not much to look at itself, but it serves as the jumping-off point for some of the...

top_locations.title: Dien Bien Phu
top_locations.snippet: Dien Bien Phu is a small town in the northwest corner of Vietnam, set in a beautiful valley near the Laotian border. It is best known as the site of the decisive battle that ended French colonial rule in Indochina. In May 1954, Vietnamese forces besieged and destroyed the Fren...

top_locations.title: Los Roques
top_locations.snippet: Los Roques is a national park archipelago of about 300 islands, cays, and coral reefs in the Caribbean Sea, roughly 160km north of Caracas. It's one of the most beautiful marine environments in the Caribbean — turquoise water, white sand, healthy coral reefs, and almost no dev...

top_locations.title: Margarita Island
top_locations.snippet: Isla Margarita is Venezuela's Caribbean playground -- a mountainous island off the northeast coast where white-sand beaches, duty-free shopping, and cheap flights from the mainland have drawn Venezuelan holidaymakers for decades. Foreign visitors are rarer now, but those who m...

top_locations.title: La Gran Sabana
top_locations.snippet: La Gran Sabana is a spectacular highland plateau in southeastern Bolívar state, stretching toward the borders of Brazil and Guyana. The landscape is unlike anything else in South America: vast rolling savanna of golden grassland punctuated by the dark vertical cliffs of tepuis...

top_locations.title: Choroni
top_locations.snippet: Choroni is a small colonial town on Venezuela's Caribbean coast, tucked into a valley at the northern edge of Henri Pittier National Park in Aragua state. Getting here from Caracas means driving through the national park itself — one of the most biodiverse areas in the country...

top_locations.title: Juan Griego
top_locations.snippet: Juan Griego is a small fishing town on the north coast of Margarita, famous for one thing: its sunsets. The bay faces west and the sun drops straight into the water, framed by the hills on either side. People gather at the waterfront restaurants each evening to watch.

top_locations.title: Tanna
top_locations.snippet: Tanna is an island in southern Vanuatu, and one of the most rewarding destinations in the Pacific for travelers willing to get off the standard tourist circuit. The island's defining feature is Mount Yasur, an active stratovolcano whose crater is one of the most accessible in...

top_locations.title: Espiritu Santo
top_locations.snippet: Espiritu Santo is the largest island in Vanuatu, a rugged, mountainous place covered in dense rainforest. The main town, Luganville, was a massive American military base during World War II — at its peak, over 100,000 troops were stationed here, and the remnants of that era ar...

top_locations.title: Ambrym
top_locations.snippet: Ambrym is one of the most volcanically active islands in Vanuatu, dominated by a vast caldera containing two live volcanoes, Marum and Benbow. These are among the most accessible active lava lakes in the world, making Ambrym a genuine destination for volcano enthusiasts willin...

top_locations.title: Efate
top_locations.snippet: Efate is the most populated island in Vanuatu and home to the capital, Port Vila. The island is ringed by coral reefs and dotted with coconut plantations, and its lush volcanic interior rises to over 600 metres.

top_locations.title: Malakula
top_locations.snippet: Malakula is the second largest island in Vanuatu and one of the most culturally rich places in the entire Pacific. Over thirty distinct languages are spoken here, a density of linguistic diversity that reflects centuries of isolated communities separated by the island's rugged...

top_locations.title: Samarkand
top_locations.snippet: The Registan is the reason most people come to Samarkand, and rightly so. Three massive madrasas face each other across a single square, their facades covered in tile work so intricate it stops you in your tracks. It is one of the finest pieces of Islamic architecture anywhere...

top_locations.title: Bukhara
top_locations.snippet: Bukhara is one of the most famous cities on the ancient Silk Road. Samarkand is maybe a bit more famous, but Bukhara wins hands down when it comes to atmosphere. This city is alive!

top_locations.title: Khiva
top_locations.snippet: Khiva's walled inner city, the Ichan-Kala, is the best-preserved medieval town in Central Asia — a UNESCO World Heritage Site of minarets, madrassas, and turquoise-tiled palaces packed within mud-brick walls. It can feel like a museum rather than a living town, and in some way...

top_locations.title: Shakhrisabz
top_locations.snippet: Shakhrisabz is Tamerlane's hometown — the place where Amir Timur was born in 1336 and where he intended to be buried. top_locations.title: Tashkent
top_locations.snippet: Tashkent is the capital of Uzbekistan but lacks the headline attractions of Samarkand and Bukhara. A devastating earthquake in 1966 levelled much of the old city, and the Soviets seized the moment — calling in volunteer workers from across the USSR to rebuild. Thousands came a...

top_locations.title: Punta del Este
top_locations.snippet: Punta del Este is South America's most glamorous beach resort — a narrow peninsula jutting into the Atlantic where the Rio de la Plata meets the ocean. It has two very different coastlines: the sheltered bay side, calm and good for families, and the open ocean side, where wave...

top_locations.title: Montevideo
top_locations.snippet: Montevideo is the very lively capital of Urugay. It is a stylish city with a strong European feel to it. The city was founded in 1726 on a promontory between the Rio del Plata and an inner bay; this area is still known as the Ciudad Vieja and is the area of main interest for v...

top_locations.title: Villa Serrana
top_locations.snippet: Villa Serrana is a small hillside village in the Lavalleja Department, about 145 km from Montevideo and 20 km beyond Minas. top_locations.title: Salto
top_locations.snippet: Salto is Uruguay's second largest city, sitting on the Uruguay River near the border with Argentina and about 500 km northwest of Montevideo. It is the centre of a major citrus-growing region, and the orange groves that surround the city give the countryside here a distinctly...

top_locations.title: La Coronilla
top_locations.snippet: La Coronilla is a tiny beach village on Uruguay's Atlantic coast, about 15 km south of the Brazilian border and just east of Parque Nacional Santa Teresa. It is the kind of place that barely shows up on maps — a handful of houses, a beach, and pine woods behind it.

top_locations.title: Kosrae
top_locations.snippet: Kosrae is the easternmost of the four states of the Federated States of Micronesia, and one of the most remote inhabited islands in the Pacific. Covered in dense jungle, flowering trees, and citrus groves, it feels genuinely untouched — there are no resorts, no cruise ships, a...

top_locations.title: Yap
top_locations.snippet: Yap is the most intriguing island in Micronesia — a place where ancient traditions are not museum pieces but everyday life. The island is famous for its giant stone money discs, some over three metres across, which still sit in stone money banks around the villages. Dance is a...

top_locations.title: Chuuk
top_locations.snippet: The islands within the Chuuk atoll are crowned with natural beauty. The outer barrier reef is punctuated with idyllic sand spits dotted with coconut palms. The high islands in the central lagoon rise into the blue island skies.

top_locations.title: Pohnpei
top_locations.snippet: Pohnpei is the largest and tallest island in the Federated States of Micronesia, and one of the wettest places on earth — its peaks collect enough rain to feed over 40 rivers and waterfalls that cascade through dense tropical forest. The island is the seat of the national capi...

top_locations.title: Majuro
top_locations.snippet: Majuro is the capital atoll of the Marshall Islands, a long, narrow ring of coral islets enclosing a large lagoon in the central Pacific. top_locations.title: Bikini Atoll
top_locations.snippet: Bikini Atoll is a UNESCO World Heritage site and one of the most consequential places in the Pacific. Between 1946 and 1958, the United States detonated 23 nuclear weapons here, including Castle Bravo in 1954 — the largest US nuclear test ever, a thousand times more powerful t...

top_locations.title: Arno Atoll
top_locations.snippet: Arno is the closest atoll to Majuro, lying just a short boat ride to the southeast, and it is one of the most accessible outer islands in the country. The atoll has over 130 islets enclosing a large, shallow lagoon with clear water and healthy coral.

top_locations.title: Jaluit Atoll
top_locations.snippet: Jaluit was the administrative capital of the Marshall Islands under both German and Japanese colonial rule, and the remnants of that history are scattered across the atoll. Japanese fortifications, a seaplane base, and the ruins of the colonial administration are still visible...

top_locations.title: Kwajalein Atoll
top_locations.snippet: Kwajalein Atoll consists of 97 islands with a total land mass of just 6.5 square miles, surrounding an immense 1,100-square-mile lagoon — the largest coral atoll in the world. top_locations.title: Saipan
top_locations.snippet: Saipan is the largest and most populous island in the Northern Mariana Islands, an American commonwealth in the western Pacific about three hours by air from Tokyo. The island saw some of the fiercest fighting of the Pacific War in 1944 — the Battle of Saipan effectively ended...

top_locations.title: Tinian
top_locations.snippet: Tinian is a small island in the Northern Mariana Islands, just south of Saipan, and one of the most historically significant — and least visited — Pacific islands. top_locations.title: St. Thomas
top_locations.snippet: St. Thomas is the busiest of the US Virgin Islands — a lush, hilly island of 32 square miles that was Danish for 250 years before the United States bought the territory in 1917 for $25 million in gold. top_locations.title: St. John
top_locations.snippet: St. John is the smallest of the three main US Virgin Islands and by far the most pristine. top_locations.title: US Virgin Islands
top_locations.snippet: The US Virgin Islands were bought from Denmark in 1917 for $25 million in gold — one of the stranger real-estate transactions in Caribbean history. top_locations.title: Hagåtña (Agana)
top_locations.snippet: Hagåtña — the old colonial name was Agana — is the capital of Guam, though you might not guess it from its size. top_locations.title: Cetti Bay
top_locations.snippet: Cetti Bay is a rugged stretch of the southwestern coast of Guam, reached by the scenic coastal road that loops around the southern half of the island. top_locations.title: Umatac
top_locations.snippet: Umatac is a historic village on the southwestern coast of Guam, set in a sheltered bay below steep green hills. It is the site where Ferdinand Magellan landed in March 1521, the first European contact with Guam, and the village celebrates this with a re-enactment festival each...

top_locations.title: Merizo
top_locations.snippet: Merizo is a small village at the southern tip of Guam, one of the most traditional Chamorro communities on the island. It sits on a calm lagoon protected by a reef, with Cocos Island visible just offshore. The pace of life here is noticeably slower than in the tourist areas to...

top_locations.title: Mangilao
top_locations.snippet: Mangilao is a village on the east coast of Guam, midway up the island and home to the main campus of the University of Guam — the largest higher-education institution in Micronesia — along with its associated Richard F. Taitano Micronesian Area Research Center, which holds the...

top_locations.title: Tutuila
top_locations.snippet: Tutuila is the largest of American Samoa's seven islands and the main base for travelers. Nearly all flights arrive here, and Pago Pago — the capital — is on Tutuila's south coast, inside the deep harbor carved by a collapsed volcanic caldera.

top_locations.title: Ofu
top_locations.snippet: Ofu is part of the Manu'a Island group, about 100 kilometres east of Tutuila and a 30-minute flight on a small plane. It's connected to its twin island Olosega by a short bridge.

top_locations.title: Alega
top_locations.snippet: Alega (pronounced Alenga) is a small village on Tutuila's south coast, about 10 kilometres east of Pago Pago. The beach here is one of the better snorkeling spots on the island.

top_locations.title: Culebra
top_locations.snippet: Culebra is a small, arid island off the east coast of Puerto Rico, reachable by ferry from Ceiba or by a short flight from San Juan — the aerial views of the cays and reefs on approach are worth the fare alone.

top_locations.title: Puerto Rico
top_locations.snippet: Puerto Rico sits in a curious political category: a U.S. territory, not a state, with residents who are U.S. citizens by birth but cannot vote in federal elections. top_locations.title: San Juan
top_locations.snippet: San Juan is Puerto Rico's capital and the largest city in the Caribbean, with a population of about one million. It sits on the northeastern coast of the island, and the contrast between its parts is pronounced: Old San Juan — a 7-square-block walled city on a small peninsula...

top_locations.title: Vieques
top_locations.snippet: Vieques is a small island off the east coast of Puerto Rico, about a 30-minute ferry ride from Ceiba. top_locations.title: Cabo Rojo
top_locations.snippet: Cabo Rojo sits at the southwestern tip of Puerto Rico, where the island tapers into a jagged coastline of salt flats, mangroves, and wind-scoured cliffs. It is one of the less-touristed corners of the island — quieter than the east coast resorts, and all the better for it.

top_locations.title: Alaska
top_locations.snippet: Alaska is the wild edge of the United States — a state larger than Texas, California, and Montana combined, with a population smaller than most American cities. Scale is the first thing that surprises visitors. The road system barely touches the interior; more than 80% of Alas...

top_locations.title: Inside Passage
top_locations.snippet: The Inside Passage is the sheltered coastal route threading through southeast Alaska's archipelago of islands, fjords, and old-growth forest. top_locations.title: Juneau
top_locations.snippet: Juneau is the capital of Alaska and one of the most unusual state capitals in the United States — it cannot be reached by road. Hemmed in by the Gastineau Channel to the east and the Coast Mountains to the west, the city is accessible only by sea or air, which gives it a front...

top_locations.title: Skagway
top_locations.snippet: Skagway sits at the head of the Lynn Canal, the deepest fjord in North America, and it exists because of gold. top_locations.title: Seward
top_locations.snippet: Seward sits at the head of Resurrection Bay on Alaska's Kenai Peninsula, backed by mountains and glaciers on three sides. It is the main gateway to Kenai Fjords National Park and one of the best places in Alaska to see tidewater glaciers, whales, and sea otters from a day boat.

top_locations.title: Kaua'i
top_locations.snippet: Kaua'i is the oldest and northernmost of the main Hawaiian Islands — an almost circular volcanic island of about 1,430 square kilometres, less developed and far greener than either Oʻahu or Maui. top_locations.title: Koloa
top_locations.snippet: Koloa is where sugar came to Hawaii. top_locations.title: Hawaii
top_locations.snippet: Hawaii is unlike anywhere else in the United States. A chain of volcanic islands in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, more than 2,000 miles from the nearest continent, it has developed a culture and landscape that feel like another country entirely. The spirit of aloha is real...

top_locations.title: Maui
top_locations.snippet: Maui is the second-largest of the Hawaiian islands and, for many travellers, the most rewarding. top_locations.title: Kihei
top_locations.snippet: Kihei stretches along the sunny southwest coast of Maui, a string of beach parks and low-rise condominiums that has become the island's most popular base for budget-minded visitors. The weather is the main selling point — Kihei sits in the rain shadow of Haleakalā and gets far...

top_locations.title: Kailua-Kona
top_locations.snippet: Kailua-Kona sits on the dry, leeward side of the Big Island — the side that doesn't get the rain. While the rest of Hawaii can be lush and overcast, Kona is reliably sunny, which is exactly why it became the island's tourist hub. The town stretches along Alii Drive, a seaside...

top_locations.title: Kailua-Kona
top_locations.snippet: Kailua-Kona is the main tourist town on the Big Island's sunny west coast, a compact strip of shops, restaurants, and historic sites strung along Ali'i Drive with the blue Pacific on one side and the slopes of Hualalai volcano on the other. The weather here is almost absurdly...

top_locations.title: Oahu
top_locations.snippet: Oahu is Hawaii's most visited and most populous island, home to Honolulu and the state capital. It's where the tourist infrastructure is concentrated — Waikiki's tower-block hotels, Pearl Harbor, and the North Shore's legendary surf breaks — but also where much of Hawaii's gen...

top_locations.title: Honolulu
top_locations.snippet: Honolulu is the capital of Hawaii and the only major city in the state, spread along the southern shore of Oahu between the Ko'olau mountains and the Pacific. For most visitors it will be the first place they arrive, and first impressions can be misleading — the high-rise spra...

top_locations.title: Haleiwa
top_locations.snippet: Haleiwa is the gateway to Oahu's North Shore and the unofficial capital of Hawaiian surf culture. The small town sits at the mouth of the Anahulu River, where a photogenic rainbow bridge marks the start of a two-lane strip of surf shops, shave ice stands, food trucks, and art...

top_locations.title: Lanai
top_locations.snippet: For nearly 70 years, Lanai — dubbed the "Pineapple Island" — was operated as a plantation by the Dole Company. top_locations.title: Molokai
top_locations.snippet: Molokai is the fifth largest of the Hawaiian islands and by far the least developed — there are no traffic lights, no buildings taller than a coconut palm, and no resort strip. Just twenty minutes by air from Maui and Oahu, it feels like a different century.

top_locations.title: Black Hills
top_locations.snippet: The Black Hills are an isolated mountain range rising from the Great Plains of western South Dakota — dark with ponderosa pine from a distance, hence the name. top_locations.title: South Dakota

top_locations.title: Deadwood

top_locations.title: “Sturgis”

top_locations.title: Aveiro
top_locations.snippet: Aveiro sits on a shallow coastal lagoon about an hour south of Porto, and its nickname — the Portuguese Venice — is well earned. top_locations.title: Óbidos

top_locations.title: Sintra
top_locations.snippet: Sintra is a small town that looks straight out of a fairy tale. Made famous by Lord Byron, Sintra was once the royal town of Portugal, and many castles and palaces can be found in its vicinity. top_locations.title: Lisbon
top_locations.snippet: Lisbon is one of Europe's oldest and most beautiful capitals, a city of seven hills falling steeply to the Tagus estuary where the Atlantic begins. top_locations.title: Algarve

top_locations.title: Évora

top_locations.title: Carvoeiro
top_locations.snippet: Carvoeiro is a small, picturesque resort village built around a sandy cove framed by ochre cliffs. top_locations.title: Douro Valley
top_locations.snippet: The Douro Valley is Portugal's great wine country — a steep, terraced landscape carved by the Douro River as it runs east toward the Spanish border. top_locations.title: Guimarães
top_locations.snippet: Guimarães is known as the birthplace of Portugal — it was here that Afonso Henriques, the first king, was born and raised, and it was from here that the country's independence was launched in the 12th century. top_locations.title: Braga

top_locations.title: Ponte de Lima
top_locations.snippet: The Romans are supposed to have thought the Lima was the mythical river Lethe, so beautiful it took men's memories away. The story goes that the legionaries would not cross until their commander swam to the far bank and proved he still remembered their names.

top_locations.title: Viana do Castelo

top_locations.title: The Azores
top_locations.snippet: The Azores are nine volcanic islands in the middle of the Atlantic, 1,500 kilometres west of Lisbon, and they feel genuinely remote. Green hills drop sharply into a dark ocean. top_locations.title: Sete Cidades

top_locations.title: Ponta Delgada
top_locations.snippet: Ponta Delgada is the administrative capital of the Azores and the main gateway to the archipelago. Most visitors arrive here first and spend a day or two before fanning out across São Miguel and the other islands — and the city rewards the pause.

top_locations.title: Sandomierz
top_locations.snippet: Sandomierz is one of Poland's oldest and best-preserved towns, perched on a loess bluff above the Vistula river. top_locations.title: Lublin

top_locations.title: Trojmiasto

top_locations.title: Toruń

top_locations.title: Krakow

top_locations.title: Wieliczka

top_locations.title: Zakopane

top_locations.title: Volubilis
top_locations.snippet: Volubilis is the best preserved Roman site in Morocco and is an easy excursion from Meknes. It is on the same winding road as Moulay Idriss, the birthplace of Moulay Idriss, the creator of the first Arab dynasty. Both sites (they are 4 km apart) are definitely worth a visit, e...

top_locations.title: Marrakesh
top_locations.snippet: Marrakesh is the most visceral of Morocco's imperial cities — an ochre-walled medina at the foot of the snow-capped Atlas Mountains where the medieval and the contemporary collide in spectacularly chaotic fashion. The city has been pulling in visitors for decades, and the tour...

top_locations.title: Essaouira
top_locations.snippet: Essaouira is the most relaxed town on Morocco's Atlantic coast — a fortified medina of whitewashed houses with blue shutters, an unbroken sweep of sandy beach, and a steady wind that has made it one of Africa's best windsurf and kitesurf spots. Marrakech sends its overheated v...

top_locations.title: Imlil
top_locations.snippet: Imlil is a Berber village at 1,740 metres in the High Atlas, about 60 kilometres south of Marrakesh and the main gateway to Jebel Toubkal — at 4,167 metres, the highest mountain in North Africa. It exists almost entirely as a trekking base: guesthouses, guide bureaux, mule hir...

top_locations.title: High Atlas
top_locations.snippet: The High Atlas is the main mountain range of Morocco and the highest in North Africa, with Jebel Toubkal reaching 4,167 metres. The range stretches roughly 700km from the Atlantic coast in the southwest to the Algerian border in the northeast.

top_locations.title: Ouarzazate
top_locations.snippet: Ouarzazate sits at 1,160 metres in the pre-Saharan south of Morocco, where the High Atlas mountains give way to the desert steppe. It is the main town and transport hub of the region and the gateway to the Draa Valley, the Dades Gorge, and the edge of the Sahara. The Moroccan...

top_locations.title: Kotor
top_locations.snippet: Kotor is the most compelling city on the Montenegrin coast — a medieval Venetian town enclosed by 4.5km of walls that climb steeply up the rocky hillside behind it. The old town is a tight maze of marble-paved lanes, Romanesque churches, and small piazzas, with cats lounging o...

top_locations.title: Bay of Kotor
top_locations.snippet: The Bay of Kotor — Boka Kotorska in Montenegrin — is one of the most dramatic stretches of coastline in the Mediterranean. The bay cuts deep into the mountains, forming a series of connected inlets that look from above like a fjord misplaced from Norway. The water is still and...

top_locations.title: Sveti Stefan
top_locations.snippet: Sveti Stefan is the most photographed spot in Montenegro — a turreted medieval village on a small island, connected to the shore by a narrow sandy causeway, with pink-sand beaches on both sides. If you've seen a postcard of Montenegro, this is probably it.

top_locations.title: Perast
top_locations.snippet: Perast is a small baroque town on the inner bay of Kotor, arranged along a single waterfront street with two small islands just offshore. It's one of the most picture-perfect places in Montenegro, and thankfully not yet overrun — though it gets busy in peak season.

top_locations.title: Herceg Novi
top_locations.snippet: Herceg Novi sits at the entrance to the Bay of Kotor, just a few kilometres from the Croatian border. It's the first town you'll reach coming from Dubrovnik, and it makes for a pleasant introduction to Montenegro — less touristed than Kotor, more authentic than Budva.

top_locations.title: Karakorum
top_locations.snippet: Karakorum (Kharkhorin in modern Mongolian) was the capital of the Mongol Empire under Ögedei Khan, founded in 1235 at the crossroads of the Silk Road. top_locations.title: Ulaanbaatar
top_locations.snippet: Ulaanbaatar — UB to everyone who goes there — is the capital of Mongolia and home to about half the country's entire population: 1.5 million people in a basin at 1,350 metres, surrounded by four sacred mountains and some of the emptiest steppe on earth. top_locations.title: Gun-Galuut
top_locations.snippet: Gun-Galuut Nature Reserve, about 130 km east of Ulaanbaatar, packs a surprising range of landscapes into a compact area: open steppe that seems to run to the horizon, the rugged Baits and Berkh mountain ranges, and the wetlands of the Kherlen River — the longest river in Mongo...

top_locations.title: Khatgal
top_locations.snippet: Khatgal is a small settlement at the southern tip of Lake Khövsgöl, the gateway to one of Mongolia's most beautiful landscapes. top_locations.title: Khentii
top_locations.snippet: Khentii is a vast, sparsely populated province in eastern Mongolia, rolling across forested mountains and open steppe toward the Russian and Chinese borders. top_locations.title: Orheiul Vechi
top_locations.snippet: Orheiul Vechi is a natural and archaeological reserve about 60 km north of Chisinau, set in a dramatic limestone canyon where the Raut river loops back on itself. top_locations.title: Chisinau
top_locations.snippet: Chisinau (also spelled Kishinev) is the capital and by far the largest city in Moldova, home to roughly a third of the country's population. top_locations.title: Tiraspol
top_locations.snippet: Tiraspol is the capital of Transnistria, the unrecognized breakaway republic that declared independence from Moldova in 1990 and has maintained a frozen existence since. The city sits on the east bank of the Dniester, about 70 km from Chisinau.

top_locations.title: Orhei
top_locations.snippet: Orhei is a small regional town about 45 km north of Chisinau. Most travelers pass through it on the way to Orheiul Vechi, the remarkable cave monastery complex that lies another 18 km beyond. Orhei itself has a modest centre with a park, a market, and a history museum.

top_locations.title: Soroca
top_locations.snippet: Soroca is a town of around 25,000 on the Dniester river in northern Moldova, close to the Ukrainian border. Its main draw is a well-preserved circular fortress built in the early 16th century by Stephen the Great — one of the finest examples of Genoese-influenced military arch...

top_locations.title: Teotihuacan
top_locations.snippet: Teotihuacan is one of the most impressive ancient cities in the Americas, located about 50 km northeast of Mexico City — roughly an hour by road. top_locations.title: Guanajuato

top_locations.title: Oaxaca
top_locations.snippet: Oaxaca (pronounced "wah-HAH-ka") is the colonial capital of the state of the same name, about 500 km southeast of Mexico City on a high, dry plateau at 1,550 m. With just under 300,000 people in the city and another half-million in the surrounding valley, it is small enough to...

top_locations.title: Mexico City
top_locations.snippet: Mexico City sprawls across the floor of a high mountain valley at 2,240 metres, the political and cultural capital of Mexico and one of the largest urban areas on the planet. Roughly 22 million people live in the metropolitan area, on the same ground where the Aztec capital of...

top_locations.title: Puebla
top_locations.snippet: Puebla de los Ángeles is one of Mexico's great colonial cities — a UNESCO World Heritage Site with over 5,000 buildings from the 16th to 19th centuries, all set against the backdrop of the snowcapped volcanoes Popocatépetl and Iztaccíhuatl. The historic centre is a grid of chu...

top_locations.title: Puerto Vallarta
top_locations.snippet: Puerto Vallarta is located in the western part of the state of Jalisco in central México, overlooking the Pacific Ocean. The second-most visited resort in all of México, Puerto Vallarta attracts over 2 million tourists per year. You will find great beaches, and lots of bars, p...

top_locations.title: Cabo San Lucas
top_locations.snippet: Cabo San Lucas sits at the very southern tip of the Baja California peninsula, at the point where the Pacific Ocean meets the Sea of Cortez. top_locations.title: San Jose del Cabo
top_locations.snippet: San José del Cabo is the quieter, more cultured half of the Los Cabos resort area at the southern tip of Baja California. top_locations.title: Sayulita
top_locations.snippet: Sayulita is a small surf town on Mexico's Pacific coast, about 40 kilometers north of Puerto Vallarta. top_locations.title: Mazatlan
top_locations.snippet: Mazatlan is one of Mexico's great Pacific coast cities — a working port with a long beach resort strip, but also a genuine old town that most visitors never bother to explore. It sits on a peninsula in the state of Sinaloa, facing some of the best sunsets on the Mexican coast.

top_locations.title: Yucatan
top_locations.snippet: The Yucatan Peninsula was the heartland of the Maya civilization, and it remains one of the most historically and naturally rich parts of Mexico. Chichen Itza, the most-visited archaeological site in the country, sits near the centre of the peninsula. But the ruins worth seeki...

top_locations.title: Riviera Maya
top_locations.snippet: The Riviera Maya is the marketing name for roughly 130 km of Caribbean coastline that runs south from Cancún airport to the town of Tulum, on the east side of Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula. In the early 1990s almost all of it was jungle and fishing villages; since then it has bee...

top_locations.title: Cozumel
top_locations.snippet: Cozumel is a small island off the coast of Yucatán, 19 kilometres across the channel from Playa del Carmen. It is one of Mexico's premier dive destinations, with the western shore fringed by the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef — the second-largest reef system in the world — and wate...

top_locations.title: Cancun
top_locations.snippet: Cancun sits at the northeastern tip of the Yucatan Peninsula, where a long barrier island — the Zona Hotelera — curves between the Caribbean and a quiet lagoon. top_locations.title: Playa del Carmen
top_locations.snippet: Playa del Carmen is the main town of the Riviera Maya, about 68 km south of Cancun along the Caribbean coast of the Yucatan Peninsula. top_locations.title: Grand Baie
top_locations.snippet: Grand Baie is the main tourist hub of the north coast — busy, convenient, and unashamedly commercial. The beach is pleasant but not the best on the island. top_locations.title: Chamarel
top_locations.snippet: Chamarel is a small village in the hilly southwest of Mauritius, best known for two of the island's most popular natural attractions: the Seven Coloured Earth and the Chamarel Waterfall. top_locations.title: Mahébourg
top_locations.snippet: Mahébourg is a fishing town on the southwest shore of Grand Port Bay, close to the international airport. It's one of the more authentic towns on the island — not heavily touristed, with a lively waterfront market and a real neighbourhood feel.

top_locations.title: Rodrigues
top_locations.snippet: Rodrigues is a small island about 560 kilometres northeast of Mauritius, and is the best reason to extend your trip. top_locations.title: Grand Gaube
top_locations.snippet: Grand Gaube is a quiet fishing village on the northeast coast, about 15 kilometres from Grand Baie. top_locations.title: Saint-Louis
top_locations.snippet: Saint-Louis was Senegal's capital before Dakar, and its former grandeur is written into every crumbling facade. top_locations.title: Chinguetti

top_locations.title: Oualata

top_locations.title: Atar
top_locations.snippet: Atar is the capital of the Adrar region and the main gateway to one of Mauritania's most rewarding corners. top_locations.title: Ouadane
top_locations.snippet: Ouadane had its glory days when the slave and gold caravans between Morocco and Ghana made their last stop here. That was long ago. Now there is just a quiet oasis town left, a UNESCO World Heritage Site slowly crumbling in the desert.

top_locations.title: Valletta
top_locations.snippet: Malta's capital is one of the smallest and most densely historic cities in Europe. top_locations.title: Mellieha

top_locations.title: Dogon Country
top_locations.snippet: Dogon Country is one of the highlights of West Africa. top_locations.title: Djenné
top_locations.snippet: Djenné is one of the oldest cities in sub-Saharan Africa and one of the most visually striking. top_locations.title: Bandiagara
top_locations.snippet: Bandiagara is the gateway to the Bandiagara Escarpment, a 200-kilometre sandstone cliff that shelters the Dogon villages. top_locations.title: Mopti
top_locations.snippet: Mopti is about halfway from Bamako to Timbuktu, spread across three islands at the junction of the Niger and Bani rivers. top_locations.title: Timbuktu
top_locations.snippet: In the West, Timbuktu means "the ends of the earth." For centuries no European saw it and returned alive. top_locations.title: Malé Atoll

top_locations.title: Malé

top_locations.title: Langkawi
top_locations.snippet: Langkawi is an archipelago of ninety-nine islands tucked against the Thai border in the northwest corner of peninsular Malaysia, and the main island shares the name. top_locations.title: Penang
top_locations.snippet: Penang — Pulau Pinang in Malay — is a 280 km² island off the north-west coast of Peninsular Malaysia, joined to the mainland by the 14-kilometre Penang Bridge and the even longer second bridge at Batu Kawan. top_locations.title: Georgetown
top_locations.snippet: Georgetown is the capital of Penang state and one of the most rewarding cities in Malaysia for travellers. top_locations.title: Cape Maclear

top_locations.title: Lilongwe

top_locations.title: Blantyre

top_locations.title: Anakao

top_locations.title: Galichnik
top_locations.snippet: Galichnik is a mountain village perched on the slopes of Bistra in western Macedonia, slowly emptying out like so many Balkan highland settlements but brought back to life once a year for its famous wedding festival.

top_locations.title: Strumica
top_locations.snippet: Strumica sits in a broad valley in southeastern Macedonia, close to the borders with Bulgaria and Greece. top_locations.snippet: Vaduz is the capital of Liechtenstein and the focus of most visits to the country. It is not a large place — the population is around 5,500 — but it has good museums, a pleasant pedestrian zone, and the royal castle looming above it all on a cliff.

top_locations.title: Malbun
top_locations.snippet: Malbun sits at around 1,600 metres in the Liechtenstein Alps, reached by a winding road from Triesenberg. It is the country's only ski resort, and its scale matches the country: a handful of chairlifts and drag lifts, a ski school, and a cluster of hotels and restaurants. The...

top_locations.title: Ghadames
top_locations.snippet: Ghadames is one of the most remarkable places in Libya — a UNESCO World Heritage oasis town on the edge of the Sahara, near the point where the Libyan, Algerian, and Tunisian borders meet. It's about 600 km southwest of Tripoli.

top_locations.title: Sabratha
top_locations.snippet: Sabratha was founded by the Phoenicians as a trading post, grew into a significant Roman port city, and today holds one of the most striking ancient theatres in the world. The three-tiered stage wall — columns rising against a backdrop of sea and sky — is the defining image of...

top_locations.title: Qasr Libya
top_locations.snippet: Qasr Libya is a small village about 45 km west of Al Bayda, in the heart of the Jebel Akhdar plateau. Its main draw is the Byzantine Museum, which holds one of the finest collections of Byzantine floor mosaics in North Africa — nearly 50 panels discovered in two sixth-century...

top_locations.title: Jebel Akhdar
top_locations.snippet: The Jebel Akhdar — "Green Mountain" — is a limestone plateau rising above the Gulf of Sirte, roughly between Benghazi and the ancient city of Cyrene. It's the most fertile part of Libya, with pine forests, juniper, and wildflowers in spring. The ancient Greek cities of Cyrenai...

top_locations.title: Al Khums
top_locations.snippet: Al Khums is a small coastal town about 130 km east of Tripoli, and for most visitors it exists for one reason: Leptis Magna, the spectacular Roman city just 3 km to the east. As the nearest town to arguably the best-preserved Roman ruins in the Mediterranean, Al Khums serves a...

top_locations.title: Monrovia
top_locations.snippet: Monrovia is the capital and largest city of Liberia, founded in 1822 by freed American slaves repatriated under the auspices of the American Colonization Society. It was named after US President James Monroe, who supported the colonization effort. That origin — the oldest repu...

top_locations.title: Harper
top_locations.snippet: Harper is the capital of Maryland County, perched on Cape Palmas at Liberia's southeastern tip where the coast turns from west-facing to south-facing. It was founded in 1834 as the capital of the independent Republic of Maryland, a colony of free African Americans, before merg...

top_locations.title: Greenville
top_locations.snippet: Greenville is the capital of Sinoe County in southeastern Liberia, about 350 km from Monrovia — the first 100 km paved, the rest dirt road. The journey is an adventure in itself and can take the better part of a day.

top_locations.title: Malealea
top_locations.snippet: Malealea is a remote village in the highlands of Lesotho, reached through the spectacular Gates of Paradise Pass — a high rock gateway that signals your arrival into a landscape of sandstone cliffs and deep valleys. It's one of the best places in Lesotho to arrange pony treks...

top_locations.title: Maseru
top_locations.snippet: Maseru is the capital of Lesotho, sitting in the western lowlands at an altitude of around 1,600 metres. top_locations.title: Baalbek
top_locations.snippet: Baalbek in the northern Bekaa Valley is one of the world's oldest cities and home to the most impressive classical ruins in Lebanon -- and arguably the most important Roman site in the Middle East.

top_locations.title: Jbeil (Byblos)
top_locations.snippet: Byblos (Jbeil in Arabic) is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, with a history stretching back over 9,000 years. Located 37 km north of Beirut, it has been occupied by Phoenicians, Egyptians, Assyrians, Greeks, Romans, Arabs, Crusaders and Ottomans, e...

top_locations.title: Deir el Qamar
top_locations.snippet: Deir el Qamar ("Monastery of the Moon") is a scenic little town on the road between Beirut and Beiteddine in the Chouf Mountains. It served as the capital of Mount Lebanon from the 16th to the 19th century and has some of the best-preserved traditional architecture in the coun...

top_locations.title: Bcharre
top_locations.snippet: Bcharre is a mountain town perched above the eastern end of the Qadisha Gorge, about 65 km northeast of Beirut. With its red-tiled roofs, olive groves and mountain backdrop, it has the feel of a Mediterranean hill village.

top_locations.title: Beirut
top_locations.snippet: Beirut is a city that refuses to stay down. Built on a rocky promontory at the centre of Lebanon's coast, it has been destroyed and rebuilt so many times that resilience is practically its defining characteristic. The civil war (1975-1990) leveled much of the city centre. Reco...

top_locations.title: Riga
top_locations.snippet: Riga is the capital of Latvia and home to around a third of the country's population — a concentration that makes it the undisputed centre of Latvian life. It's one of the most architecturally impressive cities in the Baltic region, and for most visitors it's the reason to com...

top_locations.title: Jurmala
top_locations.snippet: Jurmala is a long, low beach resort strung out along the Gulf of Riga, about 25 kilometres west of the capital. It's been a summer destination for city dwellers since the mid-19th century, when Russian aristocrats and later Soviet-era workers came here to take the sea air. The...

top_locations.title: Cesis
top_locations.snippet: Cesis is the most appealing town in the Gauja Valley and arguably the best-preserved medieval settlement in the Baltics. It's about 90 minutes from Riga by train and makes an easy day trip, though an overnight stay lets you see it more slowly.

top_locations.title: Ruhnu Island
top_locations.snippet: Ruhnu is Estonia's most remote inhabited island, a tiny speck in the Gulf of Riga closer to Latvia than to the Estonian mainland. About sixty people live here year-round, and the island has the unhurried feel of a place that time has not quite reached.

top_locations.title: Ventspils
top_locations.snippet: Ventspils is a port city on Latvia's northwest coast, about 190 kilometres from Riga. top_locations.title: Luang Prabang
top_locations.snippet: Luang Prabang is quite possibly the most beautiful small city in Southeast Asia. top_locations.title: Vang Vieng
top_locations.snippet: Vang Vieng sits on the Nam Song river between Vientiane and Luang Prabang, surrounded by dramatic limestone karst mountains honeycombed with caves. top_locations.title: Vientiane
top_locations.snippet: Southeast Asia's smallest and most laid-back capital sits on a bend in the Mekong, gazing across the river at Thailand. top_locations.title: Pakse
top_locations.snippet: Pakse is the largest city in southern Laos and the gateway to some of the country's most rewarding destinations. top_locations.title: Phonsavan
top_locations.snippet: Phonsavan is a small, chilly town on the Xieng Khouang Plateau, rebuilt after the original provincial capital was destroyed by bombing during the Vietnam War. top_locations.title: Karakol
top_locations.snippet: Karakol is the main town on the eastern shore of Lake Issyk-Kul and the trekking capital of Kyrgyzstan. top_locations.title: Bishkek
top_locations.snippet: Bishkek is a classic Soviet-planned city of wide boulevards, marble government buildings and shady parks, sitting at 800 meters on the northern edge of the Kyrgyz Ala-Too mountains. With a population of around one million, it feels spacious and green in summer, though architec...

top_locations.title: Osh
top_locations.snippet: Osh is the second-largest city in Kyrgyzstan and one of the oldest cities in Central Asia, with a history stretching back over 3,000 years. top_locations.title: Uzgen
top_locations.snippet: Uzgen is a small town on the old Silk Road in southern Kyrgyzstan, between Jalal-Abad and Osh. It is worth a stop for two things: its 12th-century Karakhanid monuments and its bazaar.

top_locations.title: Norus
top_locations.snippet: Norus is a small ski area about 35 kilometers from Bishkek, making it the most convenient option for a day on the slopes if you are based in the capital. It is not world-class skiing by any measure, but it is easy to reach and surprisingly enjoyable for what it is.

top_locations.title: Kuwait City
top_locations.snippet: Kuwait City is the capital and the only real city in Kuwait. It sits on the southern shore of Kuwait Bay, a modern skyline of glass towers rising from what was, just seventy years ago, a small walled town of mud-brick houses and pearl-diving dhows.

top_locations.title: Failaka Island
top_locations.snippet: Failaka is an island about 20 km off the coast of Kuwait City, and it is the most historically significant site in the country. top_locations.title: Salmiya
top_locations.snippet: Salmiya is Kuwait's second city in all but name -- a densely populated district about 12 km south of central Kuwait City that serves as the country's main commercial and entertainment hub. top_locations.title: Ahmadi
top_locations.snippet: Ahmadi is Kuwait's oil town, built by the Kuwait Oil Company in the 1940s and named after the ruling Emir at the time. top_locations.title: Prizren
top_locations.snippet: Prizren is one of the most beautiful towns in Kosovo, set on the slopes of the Sharr Mountains where the river Bistrica winds through the old centre. top_locations.title: Peja
top_locations.snippet: Peja (Albanian: Pejë; Serbian: Peć) sits at the mouth of the Rugova Gorge, where the Bistrica river tumbles out of the Accursed Mountains — the dramatic limestone range that marks Kosovo's border with Montenegro and Albania. top_locations.title: Pristina
top_locations.snippet: Pristina is the capital of Kosovo and a city that wears its complicated history on its sleeve. top_locations.title: Penrhyn

top_locations.title: Manihiki
top_locations.snippet: Manihiki is a remote atoll in the northern Cook Islands, about 1,200km north of Rarotonga. It consists of roughly 40 small islets ringing a large central lagoon, and the population of a few hundred lives primarily in the village of Tukao on one of the larger islets.

top_locations.title: Masai Mara N.R.
top_locations.snippet: The Masai Mara is Kenya's most famous wildlife reserve, a 1,510 square-kilometre slice of savanna in the southwest of the country that forms the northern edge of the much larger Serengeti ecosystem across the border in Tanzania. top_locations.title: The Rift Valley
top_locations.snippet: The Rift Valley is the dominant geological feature of Kenya. top_locations.title: Narok Town
top_locations.snippet: Narok is the last proper town on the road to the Masai Mara from Nairobi — about halfway, roughly 140 km out, at the top of the escarpment where the Rift Valley falls away toward the reserve. top_locations.title: Nakuru
top_locations.snippet: Nakuru is Kenya's fourth-largest city and the unofficial capital of the Rift Valley — a busy agricultural hub on the floor of the Great Rift, ringed by volcanoes, soda lakes, and farmland. top_locations.title: Lake Naivasha
top_locations.snippet: Lake Naivasha is one of Kenya's few freshwater lakes, sitting at about 1,880 metres in the Rift Valley northwest of Nairobi. top_locations.title: Mombasa
top_locations.snippet: Mombasa is Kenya’s second city and the busiest port in East Africa, an island of nearly 1.3 million people wrapped in Indian Ocean creeks on the country’s southern coast. top_locations.title: Tsavo N.P.

top_locations.title: Watamu
top_locations.snippet: Watamu is a small beach village on Kenya's coast, about 20 km south of Malindi and roughly 120 km north of Mombasa. top_locations.title: Lamu
top_locations.snippet: Lamu is the oldest living town in Kenya, a Swahili settlement on a small island off the northern coast that has barely changed in centuries. top_locations.title: South of Mombasa

top_locations.title: Almaty

top_locations.title: Turkestan

top_locations.snippet: Wadi Rum is Lawrence of Arabia country. A vast desert landscape of dry riverbeds, natural rock bridges, high mountains, and wind-swept black hills stretching to the horizon. top_locations.title: Jerash

top_locations.title: Amman

top_locations.title: Hokkaido

top_locations.title: Kyushu

top_locations.title: Beppu

top_locations.title: Kumamoto
top_locations.snippet: The third-largest city in Kyushu after Fukuoka and Kitakyushu, Kumamoto sits on the central plains of the island with the ancient volcanic plateau of Aso-san rising to the east. top_locations.title: Kagoshima
top_locations.snippet: Kagoshima faces one of the most dramatic urban backdrops in Japan: Sakurajima, an active volcano that regularly dusts the city in fine ash. top_locations.title: Shikoku

top_locations.title: Takamatsu

top_locations.title: Nikkō

top_locations.title: Tohoku

top_locations.title: Sendai
top_locations.snippet: Sendai is the largest city in the Tohoku region and the natural base for exploring northern Honshu. top_locations.title: Iwate
top_locations.snippet: Iwate is the second largest prefecture in Japan by area and one of the least densely populated, covering a large stretch of northern Honshu between the mountains and the Pacific coast. It sits at the heart of the Tohoku region.

top_locations.title: Niigata
top_locations.snippet: Niigata is the largest city on the Sea of Japan coast of Honshu, about two hours by Shinkansen from Tokyo. For most foreign visitors it is a stopover rather than a destination — the port where the ferries leave for Sado Island, or the gateway to the ski resorts of the Echigo-Y...

top_locations.title: Kansai
top_locations.snippet: Kansai (also called Kinki) is the cultural heartland of Japan — the region that gave the country most of its history, religion, and aesthetic tradition. top_locations.title: Osaka
top_locations.snippet: Osaka is Japan's third-largest city and its most extroverted. Where Tokyo is polished and Kyoto is refined, Osaka is loud, friendly, and proud of its food. top_locations.title: Himeji

top_locations.title: Kobe

top_locations.title: Tokyo

top_locations.title: Kawasaki

top_locations.title: Takayama
top_locations.snippet: Takayama (often called Hida-Takayama) is a beautifully preserved castle town deep in the mountains of Gifu Prefecture, sometimes called "Little Kyoto" for its Edo-period merchant streets and traditional atmosphere. top_locations.title: Kanazawa

top_locations.title: Matsumoto

top_locations.title: Honshu
top_locations.snippet: Honshu is Japan's main island and home to most of what visitors come to see. It stretches over 1,300 kilometers from the subtropical south to the snowy north, and contains the country's biggest cities, most sacred temples, and finest landscapes.

top_locations.title: Bibbona

top_locations.title: Riomaggiore
top_locations.snippet: Riomaggiore is the southernmost of the Cinque Terre villages, clustered in a narrow valley where the Rivus Major stream once ran down to the sea. top_locations.title: Terracina

top_locations.title: Caserta

top_locations.title: Pantelleria

top_locations.title: Pelagian Islands
top_locations.snippet: The islands of Lampedusa and Linosa, together with the uninhabited rock of Lampione, make up the Pelagian archipelago. They lie some 200km south of Sicily and are geographically part of Africa.

top_locations.title: Lampedusa
top_locations.snippet: Lampedusa sits closer to Tunisia than to Sicily, and the landscape makes no secret of it. Flat, sun-scorched rock, wild rosemary, and a sea that turns an improbable shade of turquoise — this small island belongs geologically to Africa, even if it flies the Italian flag.

top_locations.title: Linosa

top_locations.title: Sicily
top_locations.snippet: Sicily is not just another Italian region. top_locations.title: Cefalù
top_locations.snippet: Cefalù is a small Norman town on Sicily's north coast, squeezed between a vast golden-sand beach and a sheer limestone rock that drops almost vertically into the sea. top_locations.title: Palermo
top_locations.snippet: Palermo is the capital of Sicily and its largest city, set in the Conca d'Oro — a wide bay between the sea and a ring of limestone mountains, with Monte Pellegrino rising dramatically to the north. top_locations.title: San Vito Lo Capo
top_locations.snippet: San Vito Lo Capo has one of the most beautiful beaches in Italy: a wide crescent of white sand with turquoise water, backed by the dramatic Monte Monaco. top_locations.title: Agrigento

top_locations.title: Taormina

top_locations.title: Aeolian Islands
top_locations.snippet: The Aeolian Islands are a volcanic archipelago just north of Sicily. All seven inhabited islands are of volcanic origin, and on most of them some volcanic activity can still be experienced.

top_locations.title: Lipari

top_locations.title: Ragusa
top_locations.snippet: Ragusa is really two towns in one. The upper town, Ragusa Superiore, is modern and orderly. top_locations.title: Sardinia

top_locations.title: Alghero

top_locations.title: Cagliari

top_locations.title: Isola di San Pietro

top_locations.title: Costa Smeralda

top_locations.title: La Maddalena
top_locations.snippet: The La Maddalena Archipelago is a national park comprising around 60 islands and islets off the northeastern tip of Sardinia, a short ferry crossing from Palau. The two largest islands are La Maddalena (where the main town is) and Caprera, connected by a causeway.

top_locations.title: Porto Cervo

top_locations.title: Olbia

top_locations.title: Castelsardo

top_locations.title: Tel Aviv

top_locations.title: Acre

top_locations.title: Eilat

top_locations.title: Haifa
top_locations.snippet: Haifa is the third biggest city of Israel and the economic powerhouse of the country. As the people in Haifa say: Jerusalem is for praying, Tel Aviv for partying, Haifa for working.

top_locations.title: Ein Gedi

top_locations.title: Gaza Strip

top_locations.title: Hebron

top_locations.title: Jericho

top_locations.title: Karbala

top_locations.title: Sulawesi

top_locations.title: Kochi

top_locations.title: Leh
top_locations.snippet: Leh is the principal town of Ladakh, the high-altitude plateau region of northern India that borders Tibet and Pakistan. top_locations.title: Jammu and Kashmir
top_locations.snippet: India's northernmost state divides neatly into three very different worlds. Jammu in the south is a Hindu pilgrimage city and the jumping-off point for the mountains. top_locations.title: Dharamsala
top_locations.snippet: Dharamsala is a hill town in the Kangra Valley of Himachal Pradesh, stretched up the forested slopes of the Dhauladhar range at elevations between around 1,250 and 1,800 metres. top_locations.title: Kashmir
top_locations.snippet: The Kashmir Valley is a broad, lake-studded bowl between the Himalayas and the Pir Panjal range — one of the most beautiful landscapes in Asia, and one of the most politically complicated. At around 1,600 m, the valley runs roughly 135 km from northwest to southeast, its floor...

top_locations.title: Rajasthan
top_locations.snippet: Rajasthan is India at its most vivid. This is the land of massive forts perched on desert ridges, palaces reflected in still lakes, and cities painted in single colors -- pink for Jaipur, blue for Jodhpur, gold for Jaisalmer, white for Udaipur. top_locations.title: Agra
top_locations.snippet: People come to Agra for one thing: the Taj Mahal. top_locations.title: Jaipur
top_locations.snippet: Jaipur, the capital of Rajasthan, earned its nickname 'the Pink City' when the old town was painted terracotta-pink in 1876 for the visit of the Prince of Wales. top_locations.title: Khajuraho
top_locations.snippet: Khajuraho’s rather isolated location makes it an ideal retreat. The main attraction for tourists is the group of temples. top_locations.title: Bundi
top_locations.snippet: Bundi is what Rajasthan must have felt like before the tour buses arrived. This small town, about 40 km from Kota, sits below the star-shaped Taragarh Fort and is filled with crumbling havelis, step-wells, and narrow lanes largely free of souvenir shops.

top_locations.title: Udaipur
top_locations.snippet: Udaipur is the most romantic city in Rajasthan, built around the clear waters of Lake Pichola and backed by the ancient Aravalli hills. top_locations.title: Jaisalmer

top_locations.title: Jodhpur

top_locations.title: Kavaratti

top_locations.title: Vik

top_locations.title: Höfn

top_locations.title: Seydisfjordur

top_locations.title: Dalaba

top_locations.title: Conakry

top_locations.title: Kinshasa
top_locations.snippet: Kinshasa is one of Africa's largest cities, home to over 17 million people and sprawling along the south bank of the Congo River directly across from Brazzaville. top_locations.title: Lubumbashi
top_locations.snippet: Located some 1,500 km southeast of Kinshasa, Lubumbashi is the DRC's second city and the capital of the copper-rich Katanga region. It sits close to the Zambian border, and in many ways feels closer to southern Africa than to the rest of the Congo. The city is relatively compa...

top_locations.title: Kisangani
top_locations.snippet: Known in colonial times as Stanleyville, Kisangani sits on the Congo River over 1,700 km upstream from Kinshasa, deep in the equatorial forest. It is a city of fading colonial architecture, dense humidity, and an atmosphere that feels genuinely remote from the rest of the world.

top_locations.title: Mbandaka
top_locations.snippet: Mbandaka sits almost exactly on the equator, on the banks of the Congo River in the northwestern DRC. It is one of the few Congolese cities accessible by river, and the journey upriver from Kinshasa, while slow and uncomfortable, is one of the great African travel experiences...

top_locations.title: Goma
top_locations.snippet: Goma commands one of the most dramatic settings of any city in Africa. It sits on the northern shore of Lake Kivu, the water a deep, improbable blue against the dark volcanic rock that forms the city's foundations, while behind it Mount Nyiragongo rises to 3,470 meters, its su...

top_locations.title: Brazzaville
top_locations.snippet: Brazzaville sits on the western shore of Malebo Pool, the vast widening of the Congo River, directly across the water from Kinshasa. It is one of only two national capitals in the world that face each other across a river. Compared to its enormous neighbour, Brazzaville is sma...

top_locations.title: Pointe-Noire
top_locations.snippet: Pointe-Noire is Congo-Brazzaville's second city and its economic heartbeat — the country's main port, its oil hub, and the liveliest place on the coast. It has a different feel from the capital Brazzaville: more open, more international, with a rough-and-ready energy that come...

top_locations.title: Impfondo
top_locations.snippet: Impfondo is the capital of the Likouala department in the far north of the Republic of the Congo, roughly 800 kilometres from Brazzaville on the western bank of the Ubangi River. It is about as far off the beaten track as you can get in Central Africa.

top_locations.title: Ngazidja
top_locations.snippet: Known to the French as Grande Comore, Ngazidja is the largest and most populous of the Comoros islands, home to around 400,000 people and to Moroni, the national capital. top_locations.title: Cartagena
top_locations.snippet: Cartagena (pop. 888 000) the most popular tourist resort town in Colombia is divided into two main parts: the Ciudad Antigua (Old City) and the Ciudad Nueva (New City). Cartagnea used to be a popular placefor the privateers of the Caribbean (the most famous being Sir Francis D...

top_locations.title: Medellin
top_locations.snippet: Medellin is the most striking Colombian city to visit. Once the most dangerous city in the world — Pablo Escobar's Medellin cartel ran it through the late 1980s — it has transformed itself more dramatically than almost any other place on the continent. top_locations.title: Santa Marta
top_locations.snippet: Santa Marta is South America's oldest surviving city, founded in 1525 on a bay where the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta drops steeply to the Caribbean. That collision of mountain and sea defines the place: snow-capped peaks loom behind tropical beaches, and the surrounding natio...

top_locations.title: Villa de Leyva
top_locations.snippet: Villa de Leyva is one of the finest colonial towns in Colombia, and it earns that distinction without effort. top_locations.title: Zipaquira
top_locations.snippet: Zipaquirá is a colonial town about 50 km north of Bogotá and one of the most popular day trips from the capital. top_locations.title: Xi'an
top_locations.snippet: Xi'an was China's capital for eleven dynasties and the eastern terminus of the Silk Road. Today it's a city of 8 million, mostly unremarkable in appearance, but it holds some of the most significant historical sites in Asia. The Terracotta Warriors alone justify the trip.

top_locations.title: Pingyao
top_locations.snippet: Pingyao is the best-preserved walled city in China — a compact Ming-era trading town in the middle of Shanxi Province, about 90 km south of the provincial capital Taiyuan, whose entire old town has survived almost unchanged since the 14th century. top_locations.title: Luoyang
top_locations.snippet: Luoyang is one of China's great ancient capitals, a city where imperial dynasties rose and fell for over a thousand years. Sitting on the banks of the Luo River in western Henan Province, it served as the capital for thirteen dynasties, making it one of the oldest continuously...

top_locations.title: Shanxi Province
top_locations.snippet: Shanxi sits in the middle reaches of the Yellow River — its name literally means "west of the mountains", referring to the Taihang range that separates it from Hebei and, usefully, distinguishes it from neighbouring Shaanxi. It is an old, dry, yellow-loess land of some of the...

top_locations.title: Yinchuan
top_locations.snippet: Yinchuan is the capital of the Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, a city of around a million people on the edge of the Yellow River with the Helan Mountains rising to the west. top_locations.title: Everest Region
top_locations.snippet: The Everest Region -- known locally as the Khumbu -- is the roof of the world, home to Mount Everest (8,849m) and some of the most spectacular trekking on earth. top_locations.title: Lhasa
top_locations.snippet: Lhasa is the capital of Tibet and one of the most extraordinary cities in Asia. top_locations.title: Tibet
top_locations.snippet: Tibet is the vast, high, thinly populated plateau at the top of the world — most of it sits above 4,000 metres, and its entire southern edge is the Himalaya. top_locations.title: Nyingchi
top_locations.snippet: Nyingchi (Linzhi) is the greenest and most lush corner of Tibet, sitting in the lower reaches of the Yarlung Tsangpo River at relatively low elevations compared to the rest of the plateau. Where most of Tibet is barren and high, Nyingchi is forested, mild, and surprisingly ver...

top_locations.title: Gyantse
top_locations.snippet: Gyantse is a small agricultural town at nearly 4,000 metres in southern Tibet, one of the least changed towns on the Friendship Highway between Lhasa and the Nepali border. top_locations.title: Shanghai
top_locations.snippet: "Paris of the Orient" was the name Shanghai earned in the early 20th century, when it was the financial capital of Asia, a haven for adventurers, exiles and gangsters, and the most cosmopolitan city in the world. top_locations.title: Hangzhou
top_locations.snippet: Hangzhou is one of China's most celebrated cities, famous since Marco Polo reportedly called it the finest city in the world. top_locations.title: Suzhou
top_locations.snippet: An hour by high-speed train from Shanghai, Suzhou has been China's city of gardens for a thousand years. top_locations.title: Qingdao
top_locations.snippet: Qingdao is a coastal city on the Shandong Peninsula facing the Yellow Sea, about 700 km southeast of Beijing. top_locations.title: Nanjing
top_locations.snippet: Nanjing (南京), the "Southern Capital," has served as the capital of China during several dynastic periods and was the seat of the Republic of China government until 1949. top_locations.title: Guilin
top_locations.snippet: Guilin is the main city of a landscape that, for a thousand years, has been the archetype of classical Chinese painting — the dreamlike karst region of Guangxi, where thousands of near-vertical limestone peaks rise straight out of rice paddies and muddy rivers. top_locations.title: Yunnan Province
top_locations.snippet: Yunnan, on the Yunnan-Guizhou Plateau in the southwest of China, is a land of natural beauty and mystery, which covers an area of 394,000 square kilometers with a population of 40,000,000. top_locations.title: Xishuangbanna
top_locations.snippet: Xishuangbanna is one of the most compelling corners of China — a subtropical region in the far south of Yunnan that feels less like China and more like Southeast Asia. top_locations.title: Kunming
top_locations.snippet: Kunming, the capital of Yunnan, is the spring city — at 1,890 metres on the high plateau of southwest China, it has a climate of mild winters, cool summers, and almost permanent sunshine. top_locations.title: Hunan

top_locations.title: Beijing

top_locations.title: Mt. Wutai
top_locations.snippet: Mt. Wutai is one of China's four sacred Buddhist mountains and the only Chinese peak mentioned in Buddhist scripture. top_locations.title: Chengde

top_locations.title: Harbin

top_locations.title: Shangri-La

top_locations.title: Dunhuang
top_locations.snippet: Dunhuang sits in the wild, wild west of China: a good 2,000 kilometres west of Beijing, in the far west of Gansu Province, right on the Silk Road that caravans took from China to the Middle East for the better part of two thousand years. top_locations.title: Kashgar
top_locations.snippet: The oasis of Kashgar, with a view of the last peaks of the western Himalayas, is the last stop in China on the Silk Road. From here you can cross to Pakistan over the Karakoram Highway or to Kyrgyzstan over the Torugart Pass.

top_locations.title: Turpan
top_locations.snippet: Turpan was one of the most important oasis cities on the Silk Road — a key stopping point on the route between China and Central Asia. Today it is a small, unhurried town where donkey carts still share the streets with cars, and the surrounding desert landscape is extraordinary.

top_locations.title: Altay Prefecture

top_locations.title: Ürümqi

top_locations.title: Hainan Island
top_locations.snippet: Hainan is China's tropical island — a large teardrop-shaped province off the south coast, roughly level with Hanoi, that the Chinese treat the way Americans treat Florida or Brits treat the Costa del Sol. top_locations.title: Yalong Bay
top_locations.snippet: Yalong Bay (Yalong Wan) lies about 20km east of Sanya on the southern tip of Hainan Island, and is widely considered the finest beach on the island. top_locations.title: Sanya

top_locations.title: Haikou

top_locations.title: Dadonghai
top_locations.snippet: Dadonghai is a compact beach resort about 3km south-east of Sanya — ten minutes by minibus, or a pleasant hour's walk along the coast. It draws a younger, more budget-conscious crowd than Yalong Bay, and has a scrappier, more lived-in feel for it.

top_locations.snippet: Taipa is one of the two main islands that make up Macau's territory alongside the peninsula. top_locations.title: Coloane
top_locations.snippet: Until 1910 Coloane was a pirates' nest. Now it is the green escape from Macau's casino towers, with parks, beaches, and hiking trails that feel a world away from the Cotai Strip.

top_locations.title: Hong Kong
top_locations.snippet: Hong Kong is one of the most exhilarating cities on earth — a vertical, electric, relentless place where East and West collide in the most productive possible way. top_locations.title: Outlying Islands
top_locations.snippet: Hong Kong's outlying islands are one of its less-visited assets. Ferries from the Central Piers make most islands accessible within an hour, and the contrast with the mainland bustle is immediate.

top_locations.title: Zinga
top_locations.snippet: Zinga is a small riverside settlement south of Bangui on the Oubangui River, which forms the border with the Democratic Republic of Congo. top_locations.title: Limbe

top_locations.title: Bobo-dioulasso

top_locations.title: Banfora

top_locations.title: Gaoua

top_locations.title: Plovdiv

top_locations.title: Veliko Turnovo

top_locations.title: Burgas

top_locations.title: San Ignacio

top_locations.title: Bruges

top_locations.snippet: Nui is one of Tuvalu's nine atolls, located roughly in the centre of the island chain. It is among the more isolated of the group, with a small population spread across a few islets around the lagoon. The main community is the village of Tanrake.

top_locations.title: Niulakita island
top_locations.snippet: Niulakita is the smallest and southernmost island of Tuvalu, a tiny speck of raised coral barely half a kilometre across.
